text: The USPSTF recommends screening for prediabetes and type 2 diabetes in adults aged 35 to 70 years who have overweight or obesity. Clinicians should offer or refer patients with prediabetes to effective preventive interventions. This is a B recommendation. Screening should be considered earlier in persons from groups that are disproportionately affected by diabetes, including American Indian/Alaska Native, Black, Hispanic/Latino, Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander, and Asian American persons.

Screening tests for prediabetes and type 2 diabetes include measurement of fasting plasma glucose (FPG), hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), or an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). Diabetes is diagnosed at a fasting plasma glucose level of 126 mg/dL or greater, an HbA1c level of 6.5% or greater, or a 2-hour post-load glucose level of 200 mg/dL or greater. Prediabetes is diagnosed at an FPG level of 100 to 125 mg/dL, an HbA1c level of 5.7% to 6.4%, or a 2-hour post-load glucose level of 140 to 199 mg/dL.

The optimal screening interval for prediabetes and type 2 diabetes is uncertain. The USPSTF suggests a screening interval of 3 years as a reasonable approach for adults with normal blood glucose levels. Shorter screening intervals may be considered for patients whose initial test results are at the higher end of normal or who have other risk factors for diabetes, such as a family history of diabetes or gestational diabetes.

The USPSTF recommends that clinicians prescribe a statin for the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease (CVD) for adults aged 40 to 75 years who have one or more CVD risk factors (dyslipidemia, diabetes, hypertension, or smoking) and an estimated 10-year CVD event risk of 10% or greater. This is a B recommendation. The decision to initiate statins in adults with a 10-year CVD risk of 7.5% to less than 10% should be individualized based on patient preferences and additional risk-enhancing factors.

The Pooled Cohort Equations (PCE) should be used to estimate 10-year cardiovascular disease risk. The PCE uses age, sex, race, total cholesterol level, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol level, systolic blood pressure, blood pressure treatment status, diabetes status, and smoking status to estimate risk. Risk-enhancing factors beyond the PCE include a family history of premature atherosclerotic CVD, metabolic syndrome, chronic kidney disease, chronic inflammatory conditions, and high-risk ethnic backgrounds.

The USPSTF recommends screening for colorectal cancer in all adults aged 45 to 75 years. This is an A recommendation. For adults aged 76 to 85 years, the decision to screen should be individualized based on overall health, prior screening history, and patient preferences. This is a C recommendation. The USPSTF recommends that clinicians selectively offer screening to individual patients in this age group rather than routinely screening all adults.

Acceptable screening strategies include stool-based tests (high-sensitivity guaiac fecal occult blood test annually, fecal immunochemical test annually, or multitarget stool DNA test every 1 to 3 years), direct visualization tests (colonoscopy every 10 years, CT colonography every 5 years, or flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 years), or flexible sigmoidoscopy every 10 years combined with annual fecal immunochemical testing. The choice of screening strategy should be based on patient preferences, test availability, and local expertise.

The USPSTF recommends screening for hypertension in adults aged 18 years or older with office blood pressure measurement. The USPSTF recommends obtaining blood pressure measurements outside of the clinical setting for diagnostic confirmation before starting treatment. This is an A recommendation. Screening should be performed annually in adults aged 40 years or older and in those who are at increased risk for high blood pressure, including adults aged 18 to 39 years with a previous elevated reading.

Proper blood pressure measurement technique includes having the patient seated quietly for at least 5 minutes in a chair with feet on the floor and arm supported at heart level. An appropriately sized cuff should be used. At least 2 readings should be taken and averaged. Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) is considered the reference standard for confirming a diagnosis of hypertension. Home blood pressure monitoring is an acceptable alternative when ABPM is not available or practical.

The USPSTF recommends screening for cervical cancer every 3 years with cervical cytology alone in women aged 21 to 29 years. For women aged 30 to 65 years, the USPSTF recommends screening every 3 years with cervical cytology alone, every 5 years with high-risk human papillomavirus (hrHPV) testing alone, or every 5 years with hrHPV testing in combination with cytology (cotesting). These are A recommendations.

The USPSTF recommends annual screening for lung cancer with low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) in adults aged 50 to 80 years who have a 20 pack-year smoking history and currently smoke or have quit within the past 15 years. Screening should be discontinued once a person has not smoked for 15 years or develops a health problem that substantially limits life expectancy or the ability or willingness to have curative lung surgery. This is a B recommendation.

The USPSTF recommends one-time screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) with ultrasonography in men aged 65 to 75 years who have ever smoked. This is a B recommendation. For men aged 65 to 75 years who have never smoked, clinicians should selectively offer screening for AAA based on the patient's medical history, family history, other risk factors, and personal values. This is a C recommendation.

An A1C goal of less than 7% (53 mmol/mol) is appropriate for many nonpregnant adults without significant hypoglycemia. Providers might reasonably suggest more stringent A1C goals (such as less than 6.5%) for selected individual patients if this can be achieved without significant hypoglycemia or other adverse effects of treatment. Less stringent A1C goals (such as less than 8%) may be appropriate for patients with a history of severe hypoglycemia, limited life expectancy, advanced complications, or extensive comorbid conditions.

Perform the A1C test at least two times a year in patients who are meeting treatment goals and who have stable glycemic control. Perform the A1C test quarterly in patients whose therapy has changed or who are not meeting glycemic goals. Point-of-care A1C testing may provide the opportunity for more timely treatment changes during the clinical encounter. A1C does not provide a measure of glycemic variability or hypoglycemia. Continuous glucose monitoring should be considered as an adjunct to A1C in appropriate patients.

Metformin is the preferred initial pharmacologic agent for type 2 diabetes. It should be initiated at the time of diagnosis unless there are contraindications. Metformin is effective, safe, inexpensive, and may reduce risk of cardiovascular events. Compared with sulfonylureas, metformin as first-line therapy has beneficial effects on A1C, weight, and cardiovascular mortality. Metformin may be safely used in patients with estimated glomerular filtration rates as low as 30 mL/min/1.73 m2.

If the A1C target is not achieved after approximately 3 months of metformin monotherapy, combination therapy with an additional agent should be considered. The choice of a second agent should be guided by patient-specific factors including cardiovascular disease, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, risk of hypoglycemia, impact on weight, cost, and patient preferences. GLP-1 receptor agonists or SGLT2 inhibitors are recommended as add-on therapy in patients with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease or indicators of high cardiovascular risk.

Insulin therapy should be considered when there is ongoing catabolism (weight loss), symptoms of hyperglycemia, A1C levels greater than 10%, or blood glucose levels of 300 mg/dL or greater. Basal insulin is typically the initial insulin regimen, with a recommended starting dose of 10 units per day or 0.1 to 0.2 units/kg/day. The dose should be adjusted by 10% to 15% or 2 to 4 units once or twice weekly to reach fasting blood glucose targets without hypoglycemia.

Criteria for the diagnosis of diabetes include fasting plasma glucose of 126 mg/dL or greater (fasting is defined as no caloric intake for at least 8 hours), 2-hour plasma glucose of 200 mg/dL or greater during an oral glucose tolerance test using a glucose load of 75 g dissolved in water, A1C of 6.5% or greater performed in a laboratory using a method that is NGSP certified and standardized to the DCCT assay, or in a patient with classic symptoms of hyperglycemia or hyperglycemic crisis, a random plasma glucose of 200 mg/dL or greater.

Categories of increased risk for diabetes (prediabetes) include impaired fasting glucose defined as fasting plasma glucose of 100 to 125 mg/dL, impaired glucose tolerance defined as 2-hour plasma glucose during 75-g oral glucose tolerance test of 140 to 199 mg/dL, and A1C of 5.7% to 6.4%. For all three tests, risk is continuous, extending below the lower limit of the range and becoming disproportionately greater at the higher end. Patients with prediabetes should be referred to an intensive behavioral lifestyle intervention program.

Time in range (TIR) is an important metric derived from continuous glucose monitoring. A target of greater than 70% time in range (70 to 180 mg/dL) is recommended for most adults with type 1 or type 2 diabetes. Time below range (less than 70 mg/dL) should be less than 4%, with less than 1% below 54 mg/dL. Time above range (greater than 180 mg/dL) should be less than 25%. Older adults and those at high risk of hypoglycemia may have individualized targets with a broader target range.

Blood pressure categories for adults include normal (systolic less than 120 mm Hg and diastolic less than 80 mm Hg), elevated (systolic 120 to 129 mm Hg and diastolic less than 80 mm Hg), hypertension stage 1 (systolic 130 to 139 mm Hg or diastolic 80 to 89 mm Hg), and hypertension stage 2 (systolic 140 mm Hg or greater or diastolic 90 mm Hg or greater). Hypertensive crisis is defined as systolic greater than 180 mm Hg and/or diastolic greater than 120 mm Hg, requiring prompt evaluation and management.

Use of antihypertensive medication is recommended for secondary prevention of recurrent cardiovascular disease events in patients with clinical cardiovascular disease and an average blood pressure of 130/80 mm Hg or higher. For primary prevention, antihypertensive medication is recommended for adults with stage 1 hypertension who have an estimated 10-year atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk of 10% or greater. For adults with stage 1 hypertension and a 10-year risk less than 10%, nonpharmacological therapy is recommended as the initial approach.

For adults with confirmed hypertension and known cardiovascular disease or a 10-year atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk of 10% or higher, a blood pressure target of less than 130/80 mm Hg is recommended. For adults with confirmed hypertension without additional markers of increased cardiovascular risk, a blood pressure target of less than 130/80 mm Hg may be reasonable. Achieving blood pressure targets typically requires combination therapy with two or more antihypertensive agents from different pharmacologic classes.

First-line agents for the treatment of hypertension include thiazide diuretics, calcium channel blockers, and ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers. For stage 1 hypertension, initial therapy with a single antihypertensive agent is reasonable. For stage 2 hypertension or when blood pressure is more than 20/10 mm Hg above target, initial therapy with two first-line agents of different classes is recommended. ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers should not be used in combination due to an increased risk of adverse effects.

Nonpharmacological interventions to reduce blood pressure include weight loss for overweight or obese patients (expected reduction of approximately 1 mm Hg per kg of body weight lost), a heart-healthy diet such as the DASH diet (reduction of approximately 11 mm Hg), sodium reduction to less than 1500 mg per day (reduction of approximately 5 to 6 mm Hg), increased physical activity with at least 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise (reduction of approximately 5 to 8 mm Hg), and moderation of alcohol consumption to no more than 2 drinks per day for men and 1 drink per day for women.

In patients with clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, high-intensity statin therapy should be used to achieve an LDL-C reduction of 50% or greater from baseline. In very high-risk patients with ASCVD, an LDL-C threshold of 70 mg/dL may be used to consider the addition of non-statin therapies such as ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitors. Fasting lipid profiles are preferred for initial assessment, but non-fasting samples can be used for screening purposes as triglyceride levels are minimally affected in the non-fasting state.

High-intensity statin therapy is defined as a daily dose that lowers LDL-C by approximately 50% or greater, including atorvastatin 40 to 80 mg or rosuvastatin 20 to 40 mg. Moderate-intensity statin therapy lowers LDL-C by approximately 30% to 49%, including atorvastatin 10 to 20 mg, rosuvastatin 5 to 10 mg, simvastatin 20 to 40 mg, or pravastatin 40 to 80 mg. Low-intensity statin therapy lowers LDL-C by less than 30%. The intensity of statin therapy should be maximized before adding non-statin agents.

In adults aged 40 to 75 years without clinical ASCVD or diabetes, the 10-year ASCVD risk should be estimated using the Pooled Cohort Equations before starting statin therapy. Risk-enhancing factors include family history of premature ASCVD, persistently elevated LDL-C of 160 mg/dL or greater, metabolic syndrome, chronic kidney disease, chronic inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, history of preeclampsia or premature menopause, high-risk race or ethnicity, and persistently elevated triglycerides of 175 mg/dL or greater.

A fasting lipid profile should be obtained at baseline before initiating statin therapy. A repeat fasting lipid profile should be obtained 4 to 12 weeks after initiating statin therapy or dose adjustment to assess adherence and response. Thereafter, a fasting lipid profile should be assessed every 3 to 12 months as needed. Total cholesterol, LDL-C, HDL-C, and triglycerides should be measured. Non-HDL-C (total cholesterol minus HDL-C) is a secondary target and should be approximately 30 mg/dL higher than the LDL-C goal.

All adults aged 6 months and older should receive an annual influenza vaccine. Adults aged 65 years and older should preferentially receive a higher dose or adjuvanted influenza vaccine, including high-dose inactivated influenza vaccine, recombinant influenza vaccine, or adjuvanted inactivated influenza vaccine. If none of these preferentially recommended vaccines are available, any other age-appropriate influenza vaccine should be used. Influenza vaccination should be offered as early as September or October and continued throughout the influenza season.

Adults aged 65 years or older who have not previously received a conjugate pneumococcal vaccine or whose previous vaccination history is unknown should receive a dose of PCV20. Alternatively, a dose of PCV15 followed by PPSV23 at least 1 year later can be administered. Adults aged 19 to 64 years with certain underlying medical conditions or risk factors, including chronic heart disease, chronic lung disease, diabetes mellitus, alcoholism, chronic liver disease, cigarette smoking, cerebrospinal fluid leak, or cochlear implant should also receive pneumococcal vaccination.

All adults who have not received a dose of Tdap should receive one dose regardless of interval since the last tetanus or diphtheria toxoid-containing vaccine. Adults should then receive a Td or Tdap booster every 10 years. Pregnant persons should receive one dose of Tdap during each pregnancy, preferably during the early part of gestational weeks 27 through 36, to maximize passive antibody transfer to the infant. Wound management guidelines recommend Tdap or Td for persons with wounds who have not received a tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine within the previous 5 years.

Universal hepatitis B vaccination is recommended for all adults aged 19 to 59 years. For adults aged 60 years and older, vaccination is recommended for those with risk factors for hepatitis B virus infection. Adults aged 60 years and older without known risk factors may also receive hepatitis B vaccine. Available vaccines include the 3-dose series of single-antigen hepatitis B vaccine (Engerix-B or Heplisav-B) and the 2-dose series of Heplisav-B given at 0 and 1 month. PreHevbrio is a 3-antigen hepatitis B vaccine administered in a 3-dose series.

Recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) is recommended for adults aged 50 years and older for the prevention of herpes zoster and its complications, regardless of previous episode of herpes zoster or receipt of the previous live zoster vaccine (Zostavax). Shingrix is also recommended for adults aged 19 years and older who are or will be immunodeficient or immunosuppressed due to disease or therapy. The vaccine is administered as a 2-dose series with the second dose given 2 to 6 months after the first dose.

Chronic diseases, including heart disease, cancer, and diabetes, are the leading causes of death and disability in the United States and are leading drivers of health care costs. Six in ten adults in the United States have a chronic disease, and four in ten adults have two or more chronic diseases. Many chronic diseases can be prevented through reducing risk factors such as tobacco use, poor nutrition, physical inactivity, and excessive alcohol use. Clinical preventive services such as screening tests, counseling, and immunizations can also prevent disease or detect it early.

More than 38 million Americans have diabetes, and approximately 97.6 million adults aged 18 years or older have prediabetes. The CDC-recognized National Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP) is a lifestyle change program to prevent or delay type 2 diabetes. The program focuses on healthy eating, increasing physical activity to at least 150 minutes per week, and achieving a weight loss of 5% to 7% of body weight. Studies have shown that the DPP reduces the risk of developing type 2 diabetes by 58% in participants and by 71% in adults aged 60 years and older.

The CDC recommends that health care providers screen all patients aged 13 to 64 years for HIV at least once as a part of routine health care. Persons at high risk for HIV should be screened at least annually. High-risk individuals include injection drug users and their sex partners, persons who exchange sex for money or drugs, sex partners of HIV-infected persons, and men who have sex with men. HIV screening should be voluntary and undertaken only with the patient's knowledge and understanding that HIV testing is planned.

Annual chlamydia screening is recommended for all sexually active women aged 25 years and younger and for older women with risk factors such as new or multiple sex partners. Annual gonorrhea screening is recommended for sexually active women aged 25 years and younger and older women at increased risk. Screening for both chlamydia and gonorrhea with nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) is the recommended approach. Pharyngeal and rectal screening should be performed based on reported sexual behaviors. Pregnant persons should be screened for chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis, and HIV at the first prenatal visit.

The USPSTF recommends screening for depression in the general adult population, including pregnant and postpartum persons. This is a B recommendation. Screening should be implemented with adequate systems in place to ensure accurate diagnosis, effective treatment, and appropriate follow-up. The Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) is a commonly used initial screening instrument, followed by the PHQ-9 for a more detailed assessment. The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale is recommended for screening during pregnancy and the postpartum period.

The USPSTF recommends screening for anxiety disorders in adults, including pregnant and postpartum persons. This is a B recommendation. The Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item (GAD-7) scale is a validated screening instrument. Screening should be implemented with adequate systems in place for diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up. The optimal screening interval is not established, but a reasonable approach is to screen when anxiety has not been previously assessed or when clinical circumstances warrant rescreening.

Screening for chronic kidney disease typically involves serum creatinine-based estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (uACR). CKD is defined as eGFR less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 or uACR of 30 mg/g or greater, persisting for 3 months or longer. Risk factors for CKD include diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, obesity, family history of CKD, age older than 60 years, and history of acute kidney injury. Patients with diabetes should have annual uACR testing as kidney disease is a common complication.

At least once a year, assess urinary albumin (e.g., spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio) and estimated glomerular filtration rate in patients with type 1 diabetes with duration of 5 years or greater and in all patients with type 2 diabetes regardless of treatment. Patients with diabetes and urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 30 mg/g or greater and/or an estimated glomerular filtration rate less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 should be monitored twice annually to guide therapy. An SGLT2 inhibitor should be recommended for patients with type 2 diabetes and diabetic kidney disease.

Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality for individuals with diabetes. Common conditions that coexist with type 2 diabetes, such as hypertension and dyslipidemia, are clear risk factors for ASCVD. Diabetes itself confers independent risk. For patients with diabetes and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, treatment with an ACE inhibitor or ARB is recommended to reduce cardiovascular events. Aspirin therapy (75 to 162 mg per day) may be considered as a primary prevention strategy in patients with diabetes who are at increased cardiovascular risk.

For patients with diabetes aged 40 to 75 years without atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, use moderate-intensity statin therapy in addition to lifestyle therapy. For patients aged 40 to 75 years with diabetes and ASCVD, high-intensity statin therapy is recommended with a goal of reducing LDL-C by 50% or more from baseline. For patients with diabetes and ASCVD who are judged to be at very high risk, the addition of ezetimibe or a PCSK9 inhibitor to maximally tolerated statin therapy may be considered if LDL-C is 70 mg/dL or greater.

Heart failure is classified into four stages. Stage A refers to patients at risk for heart failure but without structural heart disease or symptoms, including patients with hypertension, atherosclerotic disease, diabetes, obesity, metabolic syndrome, or cardiotoxin exposure. Stage B refers to patients with structural heart disease but without signs or symptoms of heart failure. Stage C refers to patients with structural heart disease with prior or current symptoms of heart failure. Stage D refers to patients with refractory heart failure requiring specialized interventions.

B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) are biomarkers used in the evaluation of suspected heart failure. In the ambulatory setting, BNP of 35 pg/mL or greater or NT-proBNP of 125 pg/mL or greater suggests the diagnosis of heart failure and warrants further evaluation. In the acute setting, BNP of 100 pg/mL or greater or NT-proBNP of 300 pg/mL or greater suggests acute heart failure. Serial measurement of natriuretic peptides can be used to guide management and assess prognosis in patients with established heart failure.

The USPSTF recommends that clinicians offer or refer adults with a body mass index (BMI) of 30 or greater to intensive, multicomponent behavioral interventions. This is a B recommendation. Effective intensive behavioral interventions include 12 to 26 sessions in the first year, addressing diet, physical activity, and behavioral strategies. BMI should be calculated from measured height and weight and used as a screening tool to identify adults with obesity. A BMI of 25 to 29.9 indicates overweight, and a BMI of 30 or greater indicates obesity.

The USPSTF recommends screening for osteoporosis with bone measurement testing to prevent osteoporotic fractures in women aged 65 years and older. For postmenopausal women younger than 65 years, screening is recommended for those who are at increased risk of osteoporosis, as determined by a formal clinical risk assessment tool. This is a B recommendation. The most commonly used screening test is dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) of the hip and lumbar spine. A T-score of negative 2.5 or less at the femoral neck or lumbar spine indicates osteoporosis.

The USPSTF concludes that the current evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms of screening for vitamin D deficiency in asymptomatic adults. This is an I statement. The most commonly used test for vitamin D status is serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D. While some organizations define deficiency as a level below 20 ng/mL and insufficiency as 20 to 29 ng/mL, there is no consensus on the optimal level for general health outcomes. The USPSTF does not recommend for or against routine screening.

The recommended childhood immunization schedule includes vaccines from birth through 18 years of age. At birth, hepatitis B vaccine should be administered. At 2 months, DTaP, IPV, Hib, PCV15, rotavirus, and hepatitis B vaccines are recommended. The schedule continues with doses at 4 months, 6 months, 12 to 15 months, and 15 to 18 months. School-entry vaccines at 4 to 6 years include DTaP, IPV, MMR, and varicella. Adolescent vaccines at 11 to 12 years include Tdap, MenACWY, and HPV.

The CDC recommends updated COVID-19 vaccines for all persons aged 6 months and older. Adults aged 65 years and older and persons who are moderately or severely immunocompromised may receive additional doses of the updated COVID-19 vaccine. COVID-19 vaccines may be coadministered with other vaccines, including influenza vaccines. Patients should be counseled that common side effects include injection site pain, fatigue, headache, and myalgia. These side effects are generally mild to moderate and resolve within a few days.

The USPSTF recommends that clinicians ask all adults about tobacco use, advise them to stop using tobacco, and provide behavioral interventions and FDA-approved pharmacotherapy for cessation to adults who use tobacco. This is an A recommendation. FDA-approved pharmacotherapy for tobacco cessation includes nicotine replacement therapy (patch, gum, lozenge, inhaler, or nasal spray), bupropion SR, and varenicline. Combining behavioral counseling with pharmacotherapy is more effective than either alone. Even brief advice from a clinician can increase quit rates.

The USPSTF recommends screening for unhealthy alcohol use in primary care settings in adults aged 18 years or older, including pregnant women, and providing persons engaged in risky or hazardous drinking with brief behavioral counseling interventions to reduce unhealthy alcohol use. This is a B recommendation. The Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT) and its shorter version, AUDIT-C, are commonly used screening instruments. Unhealthy alcohol use includes the full spectrum from risky drinking to alcohol use disorders.

In patients with atrial fibrillation and an elevated CHA2DS2-VASc score (2 or greater in men, 3 or greater in women), oral anticoagulation is recommended to reduce stroke risk. Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are recommended over warfarin for stroke prevention in eligible patients with atrial fibrillation, except in those with moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis or mechanical heart valves. When warfarin is used, the target international normalized ratio (INR) range is 2.0 to 3.0. Regular monitoring of renal function is recommended in patients receiving DOACs.

A comprehensive foot evaluation should be performed at least annually for all patients with diabetes to identify risk factors for ulcers and amputations. The foot examination should include inspection of foot skin and assessment of foot deformities, neurological assessment using the 10-g monofilament test along with at least one other assessment (pinprick, temperature, vibration), and vascular assessment including pedal pulses. Patients with evidence of sensory loss or prior ulceration or amputation should have their feet inspected at every visit.

Adults with type 1 diabetes should have an initial dilated and comprehensive eye examination by an ophthalmologist or optometrist within 5 years after the onset of diabetes. Patients with type 2 diabetes should have an initial dilated and comprehensive eye examination at the time of diagnosis. If there is no evidence of retinopathy for one or more annual eye exams and glycemia is well controlled, then screening every 1 to 2 years may be considered. If any level of diabetic retinopathy is present, subsequent dilated retinal examinations should be repeated at least annually.

The CDC recommends hepatitis C screening for all adults aged 18 years and older at least once in a lifetime. Screening is also recommended for all pregnant persons during each pregnancy, except in settings where the prevalence of HCV infection is less than 0.1%. Screening should be performed using an anti-HCV antibody test, followed by a nucleic acid test (NAT) for HCV RNA in those with a positive antibody result. Persons with ongoing risk factors should receive periodic testing. Current injection drug use is the most common risk factor for HCV infection.

The USPSTF recommends biennial screening mammography for women aged 40 to 74 years. This is a B recommendation. The decision to screen women aged 75 years and older should be individualized based on life expectancy, health status, and the patient's informed preferences. Women with dense breast tissue identified on mammography should be informed of this finding and may benefit from supplemental screening with breast MRI or ultrasound, though the evidence for routine supplemental screening is still evolving.

For men aged 55 to 69 years, the decision to undergo periodic prostate-specific antigen (PSA)-based screening for prostate cancer should be an individual one. Before deciding whether to be screened, men should have an opportunity to discuss the potential benefits and harms of screening with their clinician and to incorporate their values and preferences in the decision. This is a C recommendation. The USPSTF recommends against PSA-based screening for prostate cancer in men 70 years and older. This is a D recommendation.

Blood pressure should be measured at every routine clinical visit. Patients found to have an elevated blood pressure (systolic 140 mm Hg or greater or diastolic 90 mm Hg or greater) should have blood pressure confirmed using multiple readings on a separate day. A blood pressure target of less than 130/80 mm Hg is appropriate for most patients with diabetes and hypertension. For patients with diabetes and hypertension who require pharmacologic therapy, an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker is recommended as first-line treatment, particularly in the presence of albuminuria.

Test for gestational diabetes mellitus at 24 to 28 weeks of gestation in pregnant persons not previously known to have diabetes. Screen for diabetes in early pregnancy (before 15 weeks or at first prenatal visit) in those with risk factors, using standard diagnostic criteria. The one-step approach uses a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test with plasma glucose measurement fasting and at 1 and 2 hours. Gestational diabetes is diagnosed when any one of the following is met or exceeded: fasting 92 mg/dL, 1-hour 180 mg/dL, or 2-hour 153 mg/dL.

The CDC recommends blood lead level testing for all children at ages 1 and 2 years, or at ages 3 to 6 years if not previously tested. The blood lead reference value is 3.5 micrograms per deciliter, which identifies children with higher blood lead levels compared with most children. There is no safe blood lead level in children. Even low levels of lead in blood can affect learning, attention, and academic achievement. For adults, a blood lead level of 5 micrograms per deciliter or greater is considered elevated and warrants follow-up.

The USPSTF concludes that the current evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms of screening for thyroid dysfunction in nonpregnant, asymptomatic adults. This is an I statement. The thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) test is the preferred initial screening test for thyroid dysfunction. A normal TSH level generally ranges from 0.4 to 4.0 mIU/L, although reference ranges may vary by laboratory and age. Subclinical hypothyroidism is defined as an elevated TSH with normal free thyroxine (T4) levels. The decision to screen should consider individual risk factors.

High-sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs-cTn) assays are the preferred biomarker for the evaluation of suspected acute myocardial infarction. A rise and fall pattern of hs-cTn values with at least one value above the 99th percentile upper reference limit, in the clinical setting of myocardial ischemia, is diagnostic of acute myocardial infarction. Serial measurements at presentation and 3 to 6 hours later are recommended. A single hs-cTn measurement below the limit of detection at presentation has a high negative predictive value for ruling out acute myocardial infarction.

Exercise stress testing is recommended as the initial test for the evaluation of stable chest pain in patients who are able to exercise and have an interpretable electrocardiogram. Stress testing with imaging (echocardiography or nuclear perfusion) is recommended for patients who are unable to exercise or who have an uninterpretable resting ECG (e.g., left bundle branch block, paced rhythm, significant ST-segment abnormalities). Coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) is an alternative to stress testing and provides direct anatomic assessment of coronary artery disease.
